topic.name: Calculating Related Rates With Circles and Spheres

question.text: A graphic designer is animating a circle in such a way that the area of the circle is decreasing at a rate of $12\pi\, \text{cm}^2\text{/s}.$ Calculate the rate at which the circumference of the circle is decreasing at the moment when the radius is $3\,\text{cm}.$
question.explanation:
In this situation, we want to find $\dfrac{\textrm d C}{\textrm d t}$ at the moment when $r=3,$ and we are also told that $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = -12\pi.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A = \pi r^2,$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

\[ A = \pi r^2 = \pi \left(\dfrac{C}{2\pi} \right)^2 = \dfrac{C^2}{4\pi}. \]

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (A) &= \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} \left( \dfrac{C^2}{4\pi} \right) \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm dA}{\textrm dt} &= \dfrac{\textrm dC}{\textrm dt} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dC} \left( \dfrac{C^2}{4\pi} \right) \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm dA}{\textrm dt} &= \dfrac{\textrm dC}{\textrm dt} \cdot \dfrac{C}{2\pi}. \end{align}

When $r = 3 \, \text{cm},$ $C = 2\pi(3) = 6 \pi \textrm{ cm}.$ Hence, substituting $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = -12\pi$ and $C=6\pi$, and solving for $\dfrac{\textrm d C}{\textrm d t},$ we get

\begin{align} -12\pi &= \dfrac{\textrm dC}{\textrm dt} \cdot \dfrac{6\pi}{2\pi} \\[5pt] -12\pi &= \dfrac{\textrm dC}{\textrm dt} \cdot 3\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm dC}{\textrm dt} &= -\dfrac{12\pi}{3}\\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm dC}{\textrm dt} &= -4\pi. \end{align}

We conclude that the circumference is decreasing at a rate of $4\pi \text{ cm/s}.$

question.text: A spherical hot air balloon is being inflated. At a particular moment, the rate of increase in the volume of the balloon is numerically equal to four times the rate of increase in its surface area. What is the radius of the balloon at that moment?
question.explanation:
Let $r$ be the radius of the sphere, $V$ the volume, and $A$ its surface area. We wish to find $r$ at the moment when $\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t} = 4\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t}.$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the volume $V$ and the surface area $A$ of the sphere. Since $A=4\pi r^2$ and $V = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} r^3,$ the relationship between $V$ and $A$ is

\[ V = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} r^3 = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \left(\dfrac{A}{4\pi} \right)^{3/2}=\dfrac{A^{3/2}}{3(4\pi)^{1/2}}=\dfrac{A^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi}}. \]

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

\begin{align} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (V) &= \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} \left( \dfrac{A^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi}} \right) \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} &= \dfrac{\textrm dA}{\textrm dt} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dA} \left( \dfrac{A^{3/2}}{6\sqrt{\pi}} \right) \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} &= \dfrac{\textrm dA}{\textrm dt} \cdot\dfrac{A^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi}}. \end{align}

Now, since $\dfrac{\textrm d V}{\textrm d t} = 4\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t},$ we have

\begin{align} 4\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} &= \dfrac{\textrm dA}{\textrm dt} \cdot\dfrac{A^{1/2}}{4\sqrt{\pi}} \\[5pt] A^{1/2} &=16\sqrt{\pi}\\[5pt] A &=\left(16\sqrt{\pi}\right)^2\\[5pt] A &=256\pi. \end{align}

Lastly, since $A=4\pi r^2,$ we have

\begin{align} 4\pi r^2 &= 256\pi \\[5pt] r^2 &= 64\\[5pt] r &= 8. \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Related Rate With a Sphere: Word Problem

question.text: A snowball is rolling down a snow-covered hillside so that its volume increases at a rate of $40\pi\, \text{in}^3\text{/s}.$ How fast is the radius of the snowball increasing at the moment when the radius is $2.5 \, \text{in}$ in length?
question.explanation:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given \[ \dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = 40\pi\,\text{in}^3/\text{s}, \] and we want to find $ \dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}$ when $r=2.5\,\text{in}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

\begin{align} V &= \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} (V) &= \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dt} \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \right) \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} &= \dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dr} \left( \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \right) \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} &= \dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt} \cdot 4 \pi r^2. \end{align}

Now we can substitute the given information $\dfrac{\textrm dV}{\textrm dt} = 40\pi$ and $r=2.5,$ and solve for $\dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt}.$ We get

\begin{align} 40 \pi &= \dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt} \cdot 4 \pi (2.5)^2 \\[5pt] 40 \pi &= \dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt} \cdot 25 \pi \\[5pt] \dfrac{\textrm dr}{\textrm dt} &= 1.6. \end{align}

Therefore, the radius of the snowball is increasing at a rate of $1.6\,\text{in}/\text{s}$ when the radius is $2.5\,\text{in}.$
